title: Bringing it together
summary: The same hospital floor, now on Wi-Fi 7: what changes for each device, and what to plan.

opener.promise: What Wi-Fi 7 changes on the floor, in one view
opener.problem: Four features and one requirement; the decision needs one picture and a short plan.

beats.heading: The same hospital, on Wi-Fi 7

caption.headline: The same hospital, on Wi-Fi 7
caption.takeaway: Each kind of device can gain something different, once it supports Wi-Fi 7.

beats.body:
Back on the floor where we started. Workstations with 320 MHz support move large images faster on wide 6 GHz channels {{eht-max-width}} {{width-320-vs-160}}. Badges that support multi-link keep calls steadier by using more than one band {{mlo-bands}}. Location tags and badges that use Target Wake Time sleep between wake-ups, which can extend battery life {{twt-what}}.

Each gain needs support in the device, so it grows as devices are refreshed.
beats.bottomLine: Wi-Fi 7 is not one feature: each chapter addresses a different problem on the same floor, for devices that support it.
beats.sceneDescription: The hospital floor from the first chapter, full of devices and busy with traffic flowing to the access points. A label above one of each kind of device names what it can gain: workstations, faster big files on 6 GHz; phones, more speed with Wi-Fi 7 data rates; voice badges, steadier calls with multi-link; location tags, longer battery life with TWT.

callout.title: What Wi-Fi 7 brings
points: Wide 6 GHz channels, twice as wide as before{{width-320-vs-160}}
One connection with links in several bands{{mlo-bands}}
Longer battery life on supporting devices{{twt-what}}

questions.q: Which chapter matters most for us?
questions.a: Start with today’s biggest pain point: crowded bands point to 6 GHz, slow transfers to data rates, dropped calls to multi-link, and battery swaps to Target Wake Time.

beats.heading: One requirement: WPA3

caption.headline: Wi-Fi 7 requires [[wpa3|WPA3]]
caption.takeaway: Wi-Fi 7 rates, multi-link and 6 GHz all need WPA3 sign-in{{wifi7-no-wpa2}}{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}.

beats.body:
One requirement ties the chapters together. A Wi-Fi 7 connection signs in with [[wpa3|WPA3]], never [[wpa2|WPA2]] {{wifi7-no-wpa2}}, and the 6 GHz band allows only WPA3 {{wpa3-6ghz-required}}. A device that can only do WPA2 misses the Wi-Fi 7 gains in this talk: no 6 GHz and its 320 MHz channels {{320mhz-6ghz-only}}, and no Wi-Fi 7 data rates or multi-link {{wifi7-no-wpa2}}.

Older devices can stay connected during the move, through WPA3 transition mode or a separate network {{wpa3-transition-options}}, but they connect the way they did before. Moving devices to WPA3 is what unlocks the gains.
beats.bottomLine: Plan WPA3 alongside Wi-Fi 7: without it, devices still connect but miss the Wi-Fi 7 gains.
beats.sceneDescription: The same busy hospital floor. The middle access point is labeled Wi-Fi 7 sign-in: WPA3. Above the badges, phones and workstations, labels show what WPA3 unlocks for each: multi-link, Wi-Fi 7 rates, 6 GHz and its widest channels. Above the infusion pumps, a label notes that a WPA2-only device gets no Wi-Fi 7 gains.

callout.title: WPA3 unlocks Wi-Fi 7
points: Wi-Fi 7 connections sign in with WPA3, not [[wpa2|WPA2]]{{wifi7-no-wpa2}}
6 GHz and its 320 MHz channels: WPA3 only{{wpa3-6ghz-required}}{{320mhz-6ghz-only}}
Older devices: transition mode or a separate network{{wpa3-transition-options}}

questions.q: Will our older clinical devices still connect?
questions.a: Yes, if the network still offers WPA2 for them, through WPA3 transition mode or a separate network{{wpa3-transition-options}}. They stay off 6 GHz{{wpa3-6ghz-required}} and don’t get Wi-Fi 7{{wifi7-no-wpa2}} until they are updated or replaced.

cisco.text: A Cisco network offers Wi-Fi 7 only when its security meets the requirements; otherwise access points run it as Wi-Fi 6 or 6E{{cisco-noncompliant-downgrade}}. Devices that connect with WPA2 cannot use Wi-Fi 7 or multi-link{{cisco-wpa2-no-mlo}}. Cisco’s Wireless Configuration Analyzer Express includes a Wi-Fi 7 readiness check{{cisco-wifi7-readiness-check}}.

beats.heading: What to plan

caption.headline: What to plan
caption.takeaway: Inventory devices first, survey for 6 GHz, ready the wired side, and pilot with measurable targets.

beats.body:
The gains arrive as devices that support them join the network, so start with an inventory by model and firmware: 6 GHz, WPA3 mode, multi-link mode and link count, 320 MHz {{eht-max-width}} and Target Wake Time support.

Then survey before placing access points, because walls weaken 6 GHz signals more than the older bands {{6ghz-building-loss}}, and include other medical radio systems in the survey. Check switch-port speed, power budget and uplinks for the new access points, get device makers’ validation before changing bands or security, and pilot on a busy unit with measurable targets: worst-case latency, roaming and voice quality, not only throughput.
beats.bottomLine: Plan Wi-Fi 7 with the device inventory, the wired upgrades, manufacturer validation and a measured pilot, not as an access-point swap alone.
beats.sceneDescription: The camera pulls back over the whole hospital floor on Wi-Fi 7, with traffic flowing to the access points, while the planning checklist appears beside it.

callout.title: Before you roll out
points: Inventory devices: 6 GHz, WPA3, multi-link mode, [[twt|TWT]]
Survey for 6 GHz before placing access points{{6ghz-building-loss}}
Check switch ports, power and uplinks; get device makers’ validation
Pilot on a busy unit: worst-case [[latency|latency]], roaming, voice

questions.q: What share of our devices can use these features today?
questions.a: That is the first deliverable: an inventory by model and firmware. Feature support varies device by device, so build the business case on your own fleet, not on best-case Wi-Fi 7 clients.

questions.q: What about older 2.4 GHz-only or WPA2-only medical devices?
questions.a: They keep working on the older bands but gain little directly from Wi-Fi 7, and they may shape your network and security design for years{{wpa3-dual-ssid-legacy}}. Plan their replacement with clinical engineering.

beats.heading: Topics for follow-up sessions

caption.headline: Where to go deeper next
caption.takeaway: Five follow-up topics, from 6 GHz to WPA3, to turn this overview into a plan.

beats.body:
This talk set the stage. Each topic below deserves its own session with the people who will design, buy and support the network:

- **6 GHz design**, including standard power and access-point placement
- **Data rates in practice**: capacity planning for imaging and busy units
- **Multi-link readiness** of our badges, phones and workstations
- **Battery-powered devices** and Target Wake Time support
- **WPA3 migration** for clinical devices
beats.bottomLine: Pick the topic that matches today’s biggest pain point and schedule that session first.
beats.sceneDescription: The camera pulls back over the whole hospital floor on Wi-Fi 7, with traffic flowing to the access points, while the list of follow-up topics appears beside it.

callout.title: Follow-up topics
points: Capacity for imaging and busy units
Multi-link and battery support in our devices

questions.a: No. Wi-Fi 8 (IEEE 802.11bn) is still in development{{wifi8-status}}; Wi-Fi 7 is the certified generation today, and device, survey and wired work done now carries forward.
